rationale: The hypothesis posits that oculomotor nerve palsy is a specific manifestation of TBC1D32 disruption that reliably distinguishes Alsahan-Harris syndrome (ALHAS) from Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS). However, available records for TBC1D32/ALHAS document ocular motor findings such as oculomotor apraxia and nystagmus rather than isolated cranial nerve III (oculomotor nerve) palsy. Furthermore, OMIM and MalaCards define ALHAS as an autosomal recessive severe prenatal phenotype associated with life-limiting congenital anomalies, in which post-natal cranial nerve testing is typically not feasible or applicable. Consequently, there is no evidence establishing oculomotor nerve palsy as a reliable clinical diagnostic discriminator separating ALHAS from PHS.

conflicts: The hypothesis asserts oculomotor nerve palsy is a specific feature distinguishing ALHAS, whereas documented clinical evaluations indicate oculomotor apraxia and nystagmus rather than cranial nerve III palsy.

ALHAS is defined by life-limiting severe prenatal congenital malformations, limiting the clinical utility and applicability of assessing cranial neuropathies to differentiate it from viable Pallister-Hall syndrome cases.

new_directions.question_text: Do hypomorphic or non-lethal biallelic variants in TBC1D32 present with genuine cranial nerve III paresis versus supranuclear oculomotor apraxia in surviving patients?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the exact neuro-ophthalmic phenotype (supranuclear saccadic initiation failure vs. peripheral/nuclear cranial nerve III palsy) is critical to map midbrain vs. hindbrain developmental defects in TBC1D32 ciliopathy.
